surprises: Resolution is longest-prefix-first WITH BACKTRACKING, not greedy-and-commit: SELECT r.s FROM r (table r, column r STRUCT(s INT)) returns 3 by falling back to column(r).field(s) after table(r).column(s) fails; same fallback at schema level (s3.s3.y). Docs' 'longest match' phrasing understates this.

In case 1, SELECT t.t, SELECT t.t.t and SELECT t both return the identical struct {'t': 42} — prefix length 1/2/3 all denote the bare column (column / table.column / schema.table.column); field extraction only starts at part 4. Value-vs-length is non-monotone.
Quoted field names are STILL case-insensitive: t.t.t."T" and t['T'] both match field 't'. Quoting does not opt into case sensitivity for struct keys.

Aliasing a table changes the VALUE of an otherwise-identical expression: SELECT t.t FROM t.t returns the struct, SELECT t.t FROM t.t AS z returns 42 (column.field). An alias hides both the table name and the schema.table path.
Output column naming: a pure dot chain is named after the last part verbatim (case as written, e.g. 'T'); any bracket or paren form is named by the full expression text ("t['t']", '(t.t).t').
Dot vs bracket fail differently on non-structs: dot gives 'Cannot extract field ... not a struct, union, map, or json'; bracket gives an array_extract overload-resolution error.
Unresolvable multi-part prefix errors as 'Referenced table "t.t" not found!' (it reports the failed qualifier, not the whole chain).
summary: DuckDB 1.5.5 resolves an n-part dotted reference a1.a2...an by trying qualifier prefixes longest-first — (schema.table).column, then (table-or-alias).column, then bare column — committing to the longest prefix that actually binds, with the remaining parts becoming left-to-right struct_extract calls; if a longer parse fails to bind (e.g. the part after the matched table is not a column), it backtracks to the next shorter interpretation instead of erroring. Consequently both corpus cases resolve as schema.table.column plus trailing field extractions (case 1: t.t.t.t = 42 via 1 field extract; case 2: eight t's = 42 via 5 field extracts), and prefixes of length 1, 2 and 3 all denote the same bare column. A table alias removes both the table name and the schema.table path from scope, which can silently change what an expression like t.t evaluates to. All name matching — schema, table, column, and struct field, even quoted or bracketed — is case-insensitive. NULL struct values propagate NULL through field access. Error shapes: too-deep chains raise BinderException 'Cannot extract field ... because it is not a struct, union, map, or json' (dot) or an array_extract overload error (bracket); missing fields raise 'Could not find key "..." in struct / Candidate Entries: ...'; unresolvable qualifiers raise 'Referenced table "..." not found!'.
